state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of this table as a collection of objects you can touch and move around. Would adding on the difference between the first two values still give you the correct value for the star?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, I'm not sure... so you're saying I shouldn't just keep adding 9 each time? Like, the difference between 6 and 15 is 9, so I added 9 to 15 to get 24, but maybe that doesn't work for this problem? Can you explain what you mean by treating it like objects I can touch?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine each value in the table represents a different object you can physically move around. Would adding on the difference between the first two objects still give you the correct value for the star in this case?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher vaguely acknowledges the linear addition misconception but uses an unhelpful and confusing metaphor about physical objects that the student explicitly doesn't understand, and by Turn 2 the student shows confusion rather than progress toward understanding the quadratic relationship.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher uses vague language about 'objects you can touch and move around' without connecting to any concrete real-world analogy or everyday situation that would help ground the abstract mathematical concept of quadratic versus linear patterns.
